extracted.intended_audience: writers (especially small-press authors), editors, and readers interested in the Pushcart Prize and micro-fiction
extracted.subtask_description: Explains who can nominate work for the Pushcart Prize, what kinds of pieces are eligible, how winners are selected, and includes a 50-word micro-fiction writing prompt and brief guidance on writing resonant micro-fiction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Nominators and nomination limits
rubrics_metrics.description: Editors of small independent presses can nominate no more than six pieces of writing. Pushcart also accepts nominations from their staff of Contributing Editors.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Each small press editor is limited to six nominations per year; additionally, Pushcart's staff of contributing editors may also submit nominations. The page frames this as the procedural cap on submissions from small press editors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Eligible genres and forms
rubrics_metrics.description: The nominations may be any combination of poetry, short stories, essays, memoirs or stand-alone excerpts from novels.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Press explicitly welcomes translations, reprints and both traditional and experimental writing. This is a generous eligibility scope — multiple genres and forms (including novel excerpts) are acceptable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Publication timing requirement
rubrics_metrics.description: The pieces must have been published or are scheduled for publication in the current calendar year.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A submitted piece must be associated with the relevant calendar year (published or slated for publication). This timing requirement is a strict eligibility condition noted on the Pushcart site and repeated in the post.

rubrics_metrics.name: Selection process and scale
rubrics_metrics.description: Each year, Editor/Publisher Bill Henderson leads a team of contributing editors who cull through the thousands of nominations; approximately sixty works are published in the yearly anthology.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Selection is made by a staff of contributing editors under Henderson's leadership. From the thousands of nominations, only about sixty works are chosen for inclusion in the anthology, indicating a competitive, editorial-curated selection process rather than a public vote or automatic inclusion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Quality standard implied by nominations
rubrics_metrics.description: Being nominated means an editor has singled out your work as being amongst the best pieces they've published that year.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The blog emphasizes that a nomination itself is an honor because it signals editorial judgment that the piece ranks among a press's top work for the year. The post notes the likelihood of being selected for the anthology is small, but nomination alone is meaningful for reputation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reprints, translations and experimental work welcome
rubrics_metrics.description: Pushcart welcomes translations, reprints and both traditional and experimental writing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This clarifies that previously published work (reprints) and work in translation are eligible, and that the prize is open to unconventional/experimental forms as well as traditional forms — useful guidance for presses and authors deciding what to nominate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prestige and downstream visibility (value of inclusion)
rubrics_metrics.description: Although there is no monetary prize for inclusion, being included in the yearly anthology is a coveted honor; agents and publishers read the anthology closely and may discover overlooked writers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The post highlights the practical benefits of inclusion — industry recognition, discovery by agents/publishers, and the anthology's status (awards and notable lists) — which functions as a motivational/value metric for writers considering submissions or nominations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Micro-fiction / 50-word story constraint
rubrics_metrics.description: Write a story in 50 words or less on the theme 'Not What I Expected.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The blog author frames micro-fiction as a 'challenge to build a scene that resonates in fifty words or less.' Example prompts (dinner, wrong package, dating app mistake, wrong class) are given to inspire concrete situations. The post invites readers to post their 50-word stories via comments — implying a submission method for this prompt. Emphasized qualities: economy of language, a resonant scene, and adherence to the 50-word limit and theme.
